title_en: Homily on the Supper at Bethany, on Lazarus, Mary and Martha
author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: A festal homily on the Gospel account of the supper at Bethany, where the risen Lazarus reclines with Jesus and his sisters Martha and Mary serve him. The preacher uses the scene to proclaim Christ's divinity and to defend the full reality of his incarnation against Jewish objections.
argument: The homily opens with John's account of the supper at Bethany and presents Lazarus' presence at table as proof that his resurrection was real, not a phantom. It then turns to the fire Christ came to cast on earth, interpreting it as the life-giving fire of the knowledge of God, and to the confession of Martha, which it sets alongside those of Peter and John as a proclamation that Christ is the eternal Son of God, not a mere anointed man. The preacher praises the three siblings as models of faith, love and hospitality, and especially Mary's anointing of Jesus as worship of the incarnate Word. Finally he answers a Jewish objection that no one can see God and live, arguing that God can be seen as he chooses to reveal himself, and closes with a doxology to the incarnate Son, consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

outline.move: The Gospel trumpet announces the supper at Bethany, and the preacher presents Lazarus reclining at table as a public proof of his real resurrection and a spiritual feast.
Christ came to cast the illuminating, life-giving fire of the knowledge of God on the earth, and in raising Lazarus he gave the Jews a sign to lead them to salvation.
Martha's confession of Christ as Son of God is praised alongside Peter's and John's, and the preacher insists that Christ is not a mere anointed man but the eternal, consubstantial Son.
The three siblings are praised for their unbreakable love and faith, and Mary's anointing of Jesus is interpreted as worship of the living temple of the incarnate God.
The preacher answers the objection that no one can see God and live, defends Mary's act against Judas' criticism, and closes with a doxology to the incarnate Son.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: Brother of Martha and Mary, raised from the dead by Jesus and present at the supper in Bethany.

cast.name: Martha
cast.who: Sister of Lazarus and Mary, praised for her hospitality and her confession of Christ as Son of God.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: Sister of Lazarus and Martha, who anoints Jesus' feet with costly ointment and wipes them with her hair.

cast.name: John the Evangelist
cast.who: The Gospel writer, called 'son of thunder', whose account of the supper at Bethany is the homily's starting point.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The chief apostle, whose confession of Christ is paired with Martha's.

cast.name: Jacob
cast.who: The patriarch who anointed a stone at Bethel, seen as a type of Mary's anointing of Christ.

cast.name: Judas
cast.who: The betrayer, who criticized Mary's anointing and is refuted by Christ's verdict.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet cited to show that the Lord himself, not an angel, saves his people.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: The king whose Song is quoted as a prophecy of the king anointed with nard.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: The lawgiver cited for the rule that whoever touches the altar is sanctified.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: The prophet whose oracle about the still small voice is applied to Mary's quiet contemplation.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: Cited as a model of love for the poor, with whom Martha is compared.

cast.name: Lot
cast.who: The patriarch who entertained angels unknowingly, contrasted with Martha who knowingly received the Lord of angels.

cast.name: Esau
cast.who: Jacob's brother, from whom Jacob was fleeing when he anointed the stone at Bethel.

key_terms.sense: Of the same being or substance, used of the Son's relation to the Father and the Spirit
The Anointed One, understood not as a mere anointed man but as the eternal Son of God incarnate
Flesh, especially in the phrase 'the Word became flesh', denoting the reality of the incarnation
The becoming human of God the Word, the incarnation
The fire Christ came to cast on earth, interpreted as the illuminating, life-giving fire of the knowledge of God
A sign or miracle, especially the raising of Lazarus, given to lead unbelievers to faith
Resurrection, both Lazarus' raising and the general resurrection of which it is a pledge
Confession of faith, especially Martha's and Peter's confession of Christ as Son of God
Temple, used of Christ's body as the living temple of the invisible God
Ointment or perfume, especially the costly nard Mary pours on Jesus' feet
The Jews, especially those who oppose the truth and object to the Christian proclamation
The Trinity, the one uncreated and consubstantial Godhead of Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Unchanged or without change, used of the Word's becoming flesh without alteration
Without confusion, used of the union of divine and human in Christ
Without division, used of the union of divine and human in Christ

scripture: The author cites the Gospels, especially John, and the Old Testament in Greek (Septuagint) forms. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, where applicable, note the Septuagint Psalm numbering.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily within Eustathius' episcopate
Whether the homily was delivered on a specific liturgical occasion
The precise identity of the 'blind Jew' as a literary figure or a real interlocutor

_unresolved_facts.claim: Job, source_forms [Ἰώβ], who: 'Cited as a model of love for the poor, with whom Martha is compared.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἦν γάρ πως ἡ Μάρθα φιλόξενος μὲν ὡς ἀβραμιαία, φιλόπτωχος δὲ ὡς ὁ Ἰώβ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Job is cited as a model of love for the poor (φιλόπτωχος), not specifically 'love for the poor' in the abstract; the comparison is direct: Martha is 'philoptōchos as Job [was]'.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Lot, source_forms [Λώτ], who: 'The patriarch who entertained angels unknowingly, contrasted with Martha who knowingly received the Lord of angels.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅθεν οὐ λεληθότως, οὐδὲ ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ, ὡς πάλαι ὁ Λὼτ, ἀγγέλους ἐξένισεν, ἀλλ' ἐν εἰδήσει ἀγαθῇ καὶ διαθέσει τὸν τῶν ἀγγέλων δημιουργὸν καὶ κύριον ὑπὸ τὴν ὀροφὴν εἰσεδέξατο
_unresolved_facts.fix: Lot entertained angels 'unknowingly, in ignorance' (ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ), not merely 'unknowingly'—the contrast is stronger: Martha received the Lord with full knowledge and good disposition, unlike Lot's ignorant hospitality.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Isaiah (cited prophecy), how_marked: 'Introduced by 'as Isaiah said', but the words are an adapted or conflated allusion rather than a direct quotation', sections: ['u02-rem-early']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας, ἔσωσεν ἡμᾶς, ἔσωσεν αὐτούς
_unresolved_facts.fix: The citation is introduced by 'ὡς εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας' ('as Isaiah said'), but the actual quoted words 'ἔσωσεν ἡμᾶς, ἔσωσεν αὐτούς' do not match Isaiah exactly; however, the brief's characterization of this as 'adapted or conflated allusion' is itself misleading because the text explicitly marks it as direct speech by Isaiah with φησίν. The issue is that the source text presents it as a direct quotation formula, not merely an allusion.

In u01-rem-close, Jesus is quoted ('ἐμὸν βρῶμά ἐστιν ἵνα ποιῶ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πέμψαντός με' and 'τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Πατρός μου...'), but in u02-rem-close, the brief lists Jesus as a quoted speaker without specifying which saying; actually u02-rem-close contains no direct quotation of Jesus but rather the preacher's own doxology and narrative. The saying 'τί κόπους παρέχετε τῇ γυναικί' is spoken through Matthew (διὰ Ματθαίου), not directly as Jesus' voice in the same marking structure.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Martha (confession referred to again), how_marked: 'Introduced by 'and then Martha said to him' and quoted directly', sections: ['u02-rem-mid']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ τότε ἔφη πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡ Μάρθα· «ἐγὼ πεπίστευκα ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The introduction is 'καὶ τότε ἔφη πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡ Μάρθα' ('and then Martha said to him'), but this is not a 'referred to again' of the same confession—it is the same confession event, now placed in narrative sequence after the discussion of the siblings' faith. The brief creates a false distinction between two Martha voices when this is one repeated reference to the same utterance.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Peter and Martha (shared confession formula), how_marked: 'Presented as the shared formula of both Peter and Martha, quoted directly', sections: ['u02-rem-early']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πέτρος καὶ Μάρθα· «σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος·» Ἰωάννης· «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος...»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text presents Peter and Martha as sharing the formula 'σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος', but this is not a 'shared confession formula' in the sense of joint utterance—they are sequential confessors (Peter first, Martha second). The brief's 'shared' could imply simultaneous or identical wording, but the text distinguishes them as 'first Peter... second Martha... third John' with slightly different formulas (Peter/Martha: 'τοῦ ζῶντος'; the actual Peter confession in Matthew 16:16 has 'τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος' matching Martha here).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Solomon (quoted Song), how_marked: 'Introduced by 'she heard Solomon singing' and quoted directly', sections: ['u02-rem-close']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἤκουσε Σολομῶντος ᾄδοντος ὡς «οὗ ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐν ἀνακλίσει αὐτοῦ, νάρδος ἔδωκεν ὀσμήν»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The introduction is 'she heard Solomon singing as...' (ἤκουσε Σολομῶντος ᾄδοντος ὡς), not 'she heard Solomon singing' alone—the ὡς marks a comparative construction ('as [one sings] where the king...'), and the quotation itself is garbled or adapted from Song 1:12 (LXX 1:11), not a direct quotation of the Septuagint text.
